title: Source: Petrarch, Rime 190
short: A free imitation of Petrarch's sonnet 'Una candida cerva', turning a dream vision of a white hind into a weary, bitter hunt.
body: Wyatt adapts Petrarch's Rerum vulgarium fragmenta 190, in which the poet sees at dawn a white hind with golden horns under a laurel; round her neck is written in diamonds and topazes 'Let no one touch me ... it has pleased my Caesar to make me free'; at noon he falls into water and she vanishes. Petrarch's poem is a mystical, visionary sonnet about Laura, often read as anticipating her death. Wyatt keeps the hind and the collar but turns the vision into a hunt with rivals, exhaustion and futility, and changes the meaning of the inscription from freedom to possession. The text here, in Foxwell's 1913 edition, preserves the original spelling of the Egerton manuscript (BL Egerton MS 2711, fol. 7v). Tottel's Miscellany (1557) printed a different, regularised text, and the Egerton version was not printed until Nott's edition of 1815.

title: Who so list
short: 'Whoever wishes to hunt': 'list' is an old verb meaning to please or desire.
body: 'List' (OED, list, v.1) means to wish, desire or choose, from Old English lystan; it is the same word as 'listless'. The opening 'Who so list to hount: I know where is an hynde' sounds like an invitation to fellow courtiers, as if the speaker were a huntsman offering information about game. The address to other hunters establishes the sonnet's courtly, competitive world, very different from Petrarch's solitary vision. The phrase returns as 'Who list her hount' at line 9, framing the poem's two halves.

title: hynde (hind)
short: A hind is a female red deer; the deer-dear pun, conventional in Tudor verse, makes her the beloved.
body: A hind is a female deer, especially of the red deer, the noble quarry of royal hunting. In Petrarch the 'candida cerva' (white hind) is Laura. Love-hunting allegory was conventional, and the pun deer/dear was widely exploited (compare 'Der' at line 6). Some readers also hear a bawdy rhyme in 'hynde ... behinde'. The choice of royal game prepares for the revelation that she belongs to Caesar.

title: helas
short: 'Alas' in its French form, a courtly sigh; 'I may no more' means 'I can no longer (hunt)'.
body: 'Helas' is the French form of 'alas', appropriate to a courtier and diplomat like Wyatt, who served on embassies to France, Italy and the Emperor. 'May' has its older sense 'can, am able' (Old English magan). The speaker withdraws from the chase in the second line, so the rest of the poem is about his inability to let go despite this declaration.

title: vayne travail
short: Fruitless labour; 'travail' means toil, with an echo of 'travel', the long pursuit.
body: 'Travail' means painful labour or effort, and the spelling covered both 'labour' and 'journey' in Tudor English. 'Vain' means futile, and the idea returns at line 10, 'may spend his tyme in vain'. Petrarch's speaker abandons all his work to follow the hind (lasciai per seguirla ogni lavoro); Wyatt instead stresses exhaustion and the waste of effort, so that the courtly hunt becomes an image of the futile labour of service, a recurrent concern of his satires and lyrics.

title: of theim, that farthest cometh behinde
short: He is among the stragglers of the hunt, trailing far behind the leaders, perhaps behind a royal rival.
body: The image is of a hunting field, with many riders after one deer and the speaker among the last. Unlike Petrarch's solitary lover, Wyatt's speaker is one of a crowd of competing courtiers. The rhyme 'hynde/behinde' links quarry and failure, and readers attentive to the poem's eroticism have heard a sexual innuendo in the rhyme. The line's irregular movement, with the stresses crowding at its end, mimics the laggard's position in the field.

title: Der (deer, dear)
short: The spelling 'Der' carries the conventional pun on deer and dear: he cannot draw his mind from the beloved.
body: Foxwell's text preserves the manuscript spelling 'Der', which visually suggests both 'deer' and 'dear'. The construction 'my weried mynde / Drawe from the Der' makes the mind itself a hound or hunter that cannot be called off. The pun on deer/dear is a commonplace of Tudor and Elizabethan love poetry (Shakespeare plays on it in Venus and Adonis). The verb 'Drawe' may also recall drawing hounds off a scent, continuing the hunting vocabulary of the octave.

title: as she fleeth afore / Faynting I folowe
short: The exhausted lover keeps following the fleeing deer; the enjambment and broken line enact the faltering chase.
body: The phrasing places 'Faynting I folowe' at the start of line 7 after a run-on from line 6, and then breaks off with 'I leve of therefore', so the rhythm enacts both the stumbling pursuit and the decision to stop. The contradiction between the declared withdrawal (l. 2) and the compulsive following is the psychological core of the octave. In Petrarch the lover's eyes are tired but not sated; Wyatt transfers the weariness to the body.

anchor: I seke to hold the wynde
title: a nett ... the wynde
short: A proverbial image of futility (to catch the wind in a net), borrowed from Petrarch's poems of hopeless love.
body: To catch wind in a net was a classical proverb of impossible labour (Erasmus collects it in the Adagia), and Petrarch uses it of loving Laura: the close of the sestina Rime 239 begins 'In rete accolgo l'aura' ('I catch the breeze in a net'), and Rime 212 speaks of chasing the summer breeze and writing on the wind. Petrarch also puns on l'aura and Laura. Wyatt imports the line into a sonnet that otherwise follows Rime 190, so the octave closes with a Petrarchan figure of futility.

title: Who list her hount: the sestet
short: The sestet's opening echoes the first line, now as a warning to any rival.
body: The repetition of 'Who list ... hount' marks the turn (volta) at line 9, where the speaker shifts from his own exhaustion to a warning addressed to other hunters: 'I put him oute of dowbte', I assure him. Any rival will waste his time just as he has. The tone becomes knowing and cautionary, preparing for the revelation of the collar.

title: graven with Diamonds in letters plain
short: The collar's letters are set in diamonds, emblems of hardness and constancy; Petrarch's collar also had topazes.
body: In Petrarch the inscription is written 'di diamanti et di topazi'. Wyatt keeps only the diamonds, a stone associated with hardness and invulnerability (Greek adamas, unconquerable), and so with steadfastness, and also with costly royal ornament. 'Graven' means engraved, and 'letters plain' means clearly legible, so no hunter can claim ignorance. The image of a deer collared with an inscription descends from ancient tales of long-lived stags collared by Alexander or Caesar, recorded by Pliny and later writers.

title: Noli me tangere
short: Latin for 'Touch me not', the words of the risen Christ to Mary Magdalene in John 20:17, here set on a royal possession.
body: Petrarch's collar reads 'Nessun mi tocchi' (let no one touch me). Wyatt substitutes the Vulgate's Latin, Christ's words to Mary Magdalene after the Resurrection (John 20:17), which gives the inscription a scriptural, sacred authority and makes the woman's untouchability seem quasi-divine. The effect is unsettling: a phrase about the boundary between the risen body and human touch is used to mark a woman as a king's property. Some critics read the sacrilege as deliberate irony aimed at royal claims; others see simply a heightening of Petrarch's inscription.

title: for Cesars I ame
short: She belongs to Caesar: in Petrarch, God or Laura's spiritual freedom; in Wyatt, a ruler, traditionally read as Henry VIII.
body: Petrarch's hind declares that it pleased 'my Caesar' to set her free, usually understood as God, who has freed Laura from earthly bonds. Wyatt reverses the sense: 'for Cesars I ame' declares ownership, echoing 'Render unto Caesar' (Matthew 22:21). Since the sixteenth century the poem has been read biographically as about Anne Boleyn, whom Wyatt is said to have admired before Henry VIII claimed her (a story told later by his grandson George Wyatt). The identification is plausible but unproved, and editors such as Rebholz treat it with caution. Either way, the political danger of desiring what a ruler owns is the poem's point.

title: wylde for to hold, though I seme tame
short: The closing paradox: she seems tame but cannot be held, either by the speaker or perhaps by Caesar himself.
body: The final line is Wyatt's addition, with no equivalent in Petrarch. 'Wylde for to hold' means hard to hold, impossible to keep. It suggests that the hind's apparent submission is deceptive, which may imply that even Caesar's possession is insecure. The same paradox of tame and wild governs 'They flee from me', where once 'gentle, tame, and meek' creatures become wild. The couplet gives the sonnet a sardonic, epigrammatic end.

title: Form: the early English sonnet
short: One of the first English sonnets: a Petrarchan octave (abba abba) but a sestet ending in a rhymed couplet (cddc ee).
body: Wyatt, with Surrey, introduced the sonnet into English. This poem keeps Petrarch's two-rhyme octave (hynde/behinde/mynde/wynde against more/sore/afore/therefore) but closes with a sestet rhyming cddc ee, ending in a couplet, a pattern that anticipated the later English (Shakespearean) sonnet's epigrammatic close. The lines are pentameters, though Wyatt's rhythm is often irregular, and the colons in Foxwell's transcription mark mid-line pauses. Compare Petrarch's sestet, which rhymes cdecde.
